public_messages: [Hiroshi Tanaka]: The laboratory results are credible, having been certified by two independent facilities, satisfying the procedural rigor outlined in the World Anti-Doping Code. The contamination defense, while plausible in theory, has been explicitly rejected in 11 prior cases where similar claims were made but not substantiated with conclusive evidence. Under the Code’s principle of strict liability and the burden of proof placed on the athlete, the contamination argument remains unsubstantiated here. The consistent application of the 4-year ban in such cases supports the integrity and deterrence objectives of anti-doping regulations. Therefore, Option A—applying the standard 4-year suspension—is consistent with precedent and the governing rules.

[Imani Okafor]: The laboratory results, certified by two independent facilities, meet the procedural and evidentiary standards under the World Anti-Doping Code, establishing the presence of a banned substance at twice the threshold. The athlete’s contamination defense, while theoretically possible, has been uniformly rejected in 11 analogous cases due to lack of conclusive evidence, aligning with the Code’s strict liability principle. Under Article 2.5 of the Code, the athlete bears the burden of proof to demonstrate that the prohibited substance was present due to a prohibited method or intentional use, which has not been met here. Precedent and the Code’s deterrence objectives support the application of the standard 4-year suspension. The tribunal should uphold Option A to ensure consistency and uphold the integrity of anti-doping enforcement.
